overview.title: 📖 Overview: Trust Regained, and a New Chapter on Disqualified Offerings
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 31a–31b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf closes the extended discussion of chaver status by asking whether someone who abandoned those commitments can ever be trusted again — with the halakha ultimately following the most forgiving view, illustrated vividly by Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya's brief stint as a tax collector. A baraita then draws a sharp line between the one case where self-interest disqualifies a person from ruling on his own property — examining his own firstborn animal for a blemish — and several cases where it does not, because he has no real incentive to lie. A new chapter opens with a mishna distinguishing how disqualified consecrated animals are sold: most go to the public market to maximize the Temple's profit, but a firstborn or tithe offering may only be sold quietly in the owner's home, since that profit is his alone. The daf closes with a careful account of when a tithe animal's meat may legally be sold at all, softened for orphans by the principle of returning a lost item.

slides.title: 🔄 Can a Backslid Chaver Return?
slides.subtitle: Three positions on someone who abandoned their commitment to chaver status

lines.speaker: R' Meir
lines.text: If any of them retract, they are never accepted back as a chaver — ever.

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: If they retracted only privately, while still keeping up appearances in public, they are not trusted. But if they retracted openly, they may be accepted back.

lines.speaker: Alt. Version
lines.text: Some report it reversed: accepted if they kept the practice privately even before retracting; not accepted if it was only ever a public performance.

lines.speaker: R' Shimon & R' Yehoshua
lines.text: Either way, they ARE accepted back — 'Return, you backsliding children; I will heal your backslidings' (Jeremiah 3:22).

lines.speaker: Halakha
lines.text: Rabbi Yoḥanan rules in accordance with this final, most lenient pair — a retracted chaver may always return.

callout.label: Underlying value:
callout.text: A biblical verse about repentance ultimately tips the scale toward welcoming people back rather than permanently excluding them.

slides.title: 💰 Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya's Chairs
slides.subtitle: A vivid illustration of the retraction dispute in practice

steps.content: 1️⃣ The Sages needed Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya for a matter; Rabba, Rav Yosef, and four hundred pairs of scholars set out to see him
2️⃣ Hearing they were coming, he had four hundred chairs prepared for his guests
3️⃣ Word then reached the Sages that he had become a tax collector; they sent a message: 'Go to your important position — we no longer need you'
4️⃣ He replied: 'I have already repented and resigned'
5️⃣ Rav Yosef still refused to visit, following Rabbi Meir's strict view; Rabba went to him anyway, following the later, more lenient ruling

callout.label: Real consequences:
callout.text: A halakhic dispute about trust translated directly into whether two leading scholars would even set foot in a colleague's home.

slides.title: 👁️ What You May Never Examine for Yourself
slides.subtitle: A baraita distinguishes genuine conflicts of interest from apparent ones
headers: May You Rule On Your Own?
rows: Obvious self-interest — you would be tempted to falsely permit it in order to keep the animal
Your own animal dedicated to the Temple
If he regrets the dedication, he can simply have a Sage annul the vow — no incentive to lie about a blemish instead
If he wanted to avoid the tithe, he could simply blemish his whole herd beforehand — a false claim now gains him nothing extra
The food remains usable to him even while impure, during his own days of impurity — so there is little incentive to lie

callout.label: Pattern:
callout.text: Self-interest disqualifies a ruling only where lying would actually gain the person something he couldn't get another, honest way.

slides.title: 🥩 Disqualified Consecrated Animals: Market vs. Owner's House
slides.subtitle: New mishna opens a new chapter on selling blemished sacred animals

boxes.title: Ordinary Disqualified Sacrifices
items: Sold and slaughtered in the public butchers' market, weighed like non-sacred meat
Maximizing market value matters because the profit ultimately funds the Temple treasury

boxes.title: Firstborn and Tithe Offerings
items: Sold only in the owner's home, by estimate rather than weight
The profit belongs to the owner — the priest for a firstborn, the owner himself for a tithe — not the Temple

boxes.title: Resolving an Apparent Contradiction
items: 'Benefit belongs to the Temple' doesn't describe profit from the later market sale
It refers to the ORIGINAL redemption price, which rises because buyers know they can resell profitably afterward in the market

callout.label: Same principle, different owners:
callout.text: Wherever the profit ultimately lands determines how — and where — the animal may be sold.

slides.title: 📜 Selling a Tithe's Meat — Torah Law vs. Rabbinic Decree
slides.subtitle: A careful accounting of when an animal tithe offering's meat may be sold

steps.content: 1️⃣ Torah law (from Leviticus 27:33): an animal tithe offering cannot be sold only while ALIVE — after slaughter, selling its meat is technically permitted
2️⃣ The Sages decreed against selling it even AFTER slaughter, as a precaution, lest people begin selling it BEFORE slaughter too
3️⃣ Exception: an orphan's inherited tithe animal may be sold in the ordinary way outright, under the principle of returning a lost item, so its value isn't lost to spoilage
4️⃣ For an adult owner's slaughtered tithe, the meat may only be sold indirectly, by inflating the price of its hide, fat, sinews, or horns to quietly cover the meat's value

5️⃣ Why allow this indirect method here but not elsewhere? Because unlike a lulav's naturally fluctuating price (which can plausibly hide an etrog's value), an inflated price for hide or horns would be too obviously an artifice on its own — yet the Sages permitted it anyway for the tithe

callout.label: Rava's proof:
callout.text: The Torah's own juxtaposition of substitution and non-redemption — both tied to when the animal is still alive — shows the sale ban is meant only for a living animal, by Torah law.

summary.principle: Trust, once broken, can be restored through genuine change rather than permanent exclusion, and every rule about self-interested rulings or selling sacred property traces back to exactly where real incentive to deceive — or real ownership of the profit — actually lies.

flowSteps.content: 🔄 The halakha ultimately welcomes back a chaver who sincerely retracted their retraction
💰 Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya's story shows this dispute playing out in real relationships
👁️ Self-rulings are barred only where lying would actually benefit the person

columns.content: 🥩 Where the profit lands (Temple or owner) determines how a disqualified sacrifice is sold
📜 Torah law permits selling a slaughtered tithe's meat; the Sages restrict it, with mercy for orphans

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Halakhic rules about trust and sale are calibrated precisely to where real incentive or real ownership actually resides

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Meir, can an am ha'aretz who retracted from chaver status ever be accepted back?
o: Yes, always, without any conditions
No, never — once retracted, always excluded
Only if he retracted in public
Only if three witnesses approve
quiz.e: Rabbi Meir holds the strictest position: anyone who retracts from chaver status is permanently barred from ever being accepted back, regardless of the circumstances of the retraction.

quiz.q: Whose position does the halakha ultimately follow regarding a retracted chaver, and on what basis?
o: Rabbi Meir's, based on the need for strict standards
Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's, based on the verse 'Return, you backsliding children'
Rabbi Yehuda's original version only
No halakha was ever established on this question
quiz.e: Rabbi Yitzḥak of the village of Akko, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan, rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who accept a retracted chaver back in every case, grounded in the verse about welcoming back 'backsliding children.'

quiz.q: Why is a person trusted to rule on whether his own dedicated (consecrated) animal has a blemish, but not on his own firstborn animal's blemish?
o: Because dedicated animals are never subject to blemish laws
Because if he regrets dedicating the animal, he can simply have a Sage annul the vow instead of falsely claiming a blemish, removing any incentive to lie
Because firstborns are worth less money than dedicated animals
Because only priests may own dedicated animals
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that a person has no real incentive to lie about a blemish on his dedicated animal, since he could achieve the same result honestly by having his vow annulled — unlike a firstborn, where falsely claiming a blemish is his only way to keep the animal for himself.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's resolution, what does the mishna's phrase 'the benefit belongs to the Temple treasury' actually refer to?
o: Profit from the animal's later sale in the public market
The higher price the animal fetches at its original redemption, since buyers know they can resell it profitably afterward
A special tax collected from butchers
It refers to nothing practical and is purely theoretical
quiz.e: The Gemara concludes that this phrase refers to the initial redemption price paid to the Temple treasury, which rises because the animal's resale value in the market increases what a buyer is willing to pay to redeem it in the first place.

quiz.q: Why does the Torah technically permit selling a tithe animal's meat after slaughter, and why did the Sages forbid it anyway, with an exception for orphans?
o: The Torah never permits it under any circumstances

The Torah's ban on redemption applies only while the animal is alive; the Sages extended the ban after slaughter too, as a precaution, but allowed selling an orphan's tithe animal to prevent loss of its value
The Sages permitted selling all tithe animals without restriction
Orphans are exempt from tithe law entirely
quiz.e: Rava derives from the Torah's wording that the prohibition against selling (redeeming) a tithe animal applies only while it is alive; the Sages later extended this as a precautionary decree even after slaughter, but made an exception for an orphan's inherited tithe animal under the principle of returning a lost item, preventing its value from being lost to spoilage.
